new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per content word. Default: stress the final syllable (words ending in a consonant or in any vowel other than /ɔ/, /e/); words ending in /ɔ/ or /e/ (final /e/ in verbs 'extrametrical') take penult stress; a small residue of inherited Latin proparoxytones has antepenult stress (mɔnegɔ 'nun') or penult stress before a final consonant (fórbɛh 'scissors', pɛten 'comb', légor 'hare'). Not weight-sensitive. Cresci's own summary (p. 63): 'one primary stress which typically falls on the final syllable, but may also occur on the penult or antepenult'. A fixed: final syllable reading with final /ɔ, e/ extrametrical is the surface-dominant alternative; chosen lexical (unpredictable) because placement is inherited and contrasts final/penult/antepenult on the same segmental shapes. For Milanese (Western Lombard) Salvioni 1884 p. 279 says the Latin accent is generally preserved and Angiolini 1897 p. xvi lists oxytone, paroxytone and proparoxytone words — also lexical.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Cresci's symbol key lists a grave accent for secondary stress, but §3.3 as read gives no rule for its placement.
new_statements.exceptions: Inherited antepenult/penult-before-consonant words (62-63); kalýzɛn 'soot' (epenthetic /ɛ/); unstressed derivational suffixes, esp. /-ol/ (pitɔkol 'beggar'); clitic-bearing verb forms; final verbal /e/ never stressed. Milanese (Salvioni §434 pp. 279-282): stress shifts onto suffix -olo, in 1pl/2pl verb forms, and from antepenult to penult in -itare/-icare verbs (predìcca).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (content word; clitics excluded, harmony and stress word-bounded), citation forms; Camuno (Eastern Lombard, Valcamonica, 'upper part of the low valley'). Milanese statements are diachronic (Salvioni) or orthographic-pedagogical (Angiolini).
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding statement describes Camuno, the Eastern Lombard variety of Valcamonica (Cresci: 'as spoken in the upper part of the low valley'), not Milanese/Western Lombard; Glottolog 5.3's JSON for lomb1257 lists no child languoids and the page tree did not render, so no dialect glottocode is asserted for Camuno. Milanese (the prestige variety; Glottolog refs Salvioni 1884, Nicoli 1983) is covered only by Salvioni 1884 §434 p. 279 ('L'accento latino è generalmente ben conservato in milanese') and Angiolini 1897 p. xvi (tronche/piane/sdrucciole all exist) — both consistent with lexical, Latin-inherited stress.

sources.note: §434 'Trasposizione dell'accento', pp. 279-282 (PDF pp. 277-280): 'L'accento latino è generalmente ben conservato in milanese; cambia tuttavia di posto nei seguenti casi' — then lists shifts (suffix -olo, weak position, individual lexemes, 1pl/2pl verb forms) and, p. 281, that in polysyllabic verbs which would be proparoxytone in the singular/3pl 'è uso milanese di spingere l'accento sulla penultima' (predìcca, dubìtta). Diachronic (Latin > Milanese) framing; implies lexically inherited, non-fixed stress.

sources.note: 'Piccola grammatica', Par. I n. 7, p. xvi (PDF p. 20): 'Anche il dialetto milanese ha parole tronche: redè.. parole piane: mama, pedana, candéla.. e parole sdrucciole: perpètua, fìstola, vedova, codega, fólega.' Stress marked by a graphic accent; words with final geminate consonant or final long vowel (aa, ee, ii, uu) are oxytone and left unmarked. I.e. oxytone, paroxytone and proparoxytone words all exist; no positional rule.
